text: A hypothesis test is a decision, and every decision made under uncertainty can be wrong in two different ways. Understanding those two errors, and the concept of power, is what lets you plan an experiment properly instead of running it and hoping. It also explains a common frustration — we tested it and found nothing, when the test never had a fair chance of finding anything.

Reality either has an effect or it doesn't, and your test either rejects the null or doesn't — four possible outcomes. A Type I error means claiming an effect that isn't there, with probability alpha, which you set yourself, often 0.05. A Type II error means missing an effect that's actually there, with probability beta. Power is 1 minus beta — the chance of detecting a real effect of a given size, with a common target of 80 percent.

Neither error is worse in general. Approving a broken checkout page is a Type I error; failing to ship a page that would have raised revenue is a Type II error. Which one costs more depends entirely on the business.

You can measure power by brute force — simulate many experiments where the effect is real, run the test on each, and count how often it rejects. Testing a real 7.5 dollar lift on a 55 dollar average order with standard deviation 15, across 4,000 simulated experiments per setting.

Setting the effect to zero estimates the Type I error rate — about 5 percent, exactly as promised. With 30 customers per group, the real 7.5 dollar lift is detected only about 48 percent of the time — worse than a coin flip. You need roughly 64 per group to reach 80 percent power, and with 100 per group you hit nearly 94 percent.

Four things drive power. Sample size — more data narrows the standard error, and it's the lever you control most directly. Effect size — big effects are easier to detect than small ones. Noise — less variability in the metric means more power. And alpha — a looser alpha gives more power but more false alarms.

Rather than simulate every time, a standard formula gives the sample size per group using the standardized effect size d, the difference divided by the standard deviation. For d of 0.2, you need about 392 per group; for d of 0.5, about 63; for d of 0.8, just 25. Small effects need roughly 16 times the sample of large ones.

An underpowered study has two problems — it often misses real effects, and the significant results it does produce tend to overstate the true effect size. Do the sample-size calculation before collecting data, using the smallest effect you'd actually care about, and be wary of interpreting a non-significant result from a small sample as proof of no effect.

To recap: Type I errors, false alarms with probability alpha, and Type II errors, misses with probability beta, are the two ways a test can be wrong. Power, 1 minus beta, is the chance of detecting a real effect, and it depends on sample size, effect size, noise, and alpha. Simulate power or use the formula to size an experiment before you run it.
